document.title: Motion to Intervene and Protest of Eolian, L.P. et al. to PJM Interconnection, L.L.C.’s proposed revisions to the PJM Open Access Transmission Tariff
document.filer: Eolian, L.P.Antora Energy LLCCalibrant Energy ,Convergent Energy and Power LP ,Mainspring Energy ,Verrus LLC ,

pages.text:
1 
UNITED STATES OF AMERICA 
BEFORE THE 
FEDERAL ENERGY REGULATORY COMMISSION 
 
) 
PJM Interconnection, L.L.C. 
) 
Docket No. ER26-1479-000 
) 
 
MOTION TO INTERVENE AND PROTEST OF JOINT PARTIES TO COMPLIANCE 
FILING 
 
 
Pursuant to Rules 211 and 214 of the Federal Energy Regulatory Commission’s 
(Commission) Rules of Practice and Procedure,1 Eolian L.P. (Eolian), Antora Energy, Inc. 
(Antora), Calibrant Energy (Calibrant), Convergent Energy and Power (Convergent), Mainspring 
Energy, Inc. (Mainspring), and Verrus, LLC (Verrus) (together, Joint Parties) respectfully submit 
this motion to intervene and protest to PJM Interconnection, L.L.C.’s (PJM) proposed revisions 
to the PJM Open Access Transmission Tariff (Tariff) to comply with the Commission’s 
December 18, 2025 order on service to Co-Located Loads.2  
Consistent with the Request for Clarification of the Co-Location Order3 and protest in 
PJM’s prior compliance proceeding in Docket No. ER26-1088-000 filed by several of the above 
parties,4 Joint Parties respectfully request that the Commission require PJM to include minor 
additional revisions to clarify that, in any generator interconnection process in which PJM 
studies the Co-Located Load’s withdrawals from the grid for purposes of identifying network 
upgrades, including the Necessary Studies process,5 a Co-Located Load may nominate a net 
 
1 18 C.F.R. §§ 385.211, 385.214. 
2 See PJM Interconnection, LLC, 193 FERC ¶ 61,217 (2025) (Co-Location Order). 
3 Joint Parties, Request for Clarification, Docket Nos. EL25-49-000 & 001, AD24-11-000, EL25-20-000 (filed Jan. 
20, 2026). 
4 Joint Parties, Limited Protest, Docket No. ER26-1088-000 (filed Feb. 10, 2026). 
5 The PJM OATT does not resolve definitively the circumstances in which PJM will model withdrawals of a Co-
Located Load in the generator interconnection process. But because we expect that PJM may choose to study the 
combined withdrawals of Co-Located Loads that include storage, we have filed the above-cited Request for 
Clarification and are filing this limited protest to ensure that any such study process advances the principles set forth 
in the Co-Location Order and does not result in needless network upgrades.

2 
withdrawal limit in the same manner that it may nominate a net injection limit. Among other 
potential benefits, this clarification will ensure that Co-Located Loads paired with energy storage 
can use their full technical capabilities to avoid unnecessary network upgrades, thereby 
advancing the Commission’s twin goals of protecting ratepayers and advancing speed-to-power 
within PJM.  
In addition, Joint Parties request that the Commission reject or, at minimum, defer action 
on PJM’s proposed Tariff revisions that preclude loads connected to generating facilities behind-
the-meter without interconnection rights from accessing the new Firm Contract Demand 
Transmission Service, Non-Firm Contract Demand Transmission Service, and Interim Network 
Integration Transmission Service (NITS) options established in the Co-Location Order. PJM 
must allow loads served by behind-the-meter generation (BTMG) to access the Commission’s 
new transmission services in order to ensure that loads with similar willingness and ability to 
limit withdrawals from the grid have access to similar service opportunities, and that therefore 
the proposed rates are just, reasonable, and not unduly discriminatory. The Commission should 
direct PJM to further revise its Tariff as part of the BTMG replacement rate to remove the 
restrictions limiting the new transmission services to loads connected to generation resources that 
have Interconnection Agreements with PJM.  
I. 
MOTION TO INTERVENE 
Eolian develops energy generation and storage assets throughout the United States and 
has originated 27 GW of operating capacity to date. Eolian and its partners have developed 
projects supporting large loads in multiple regions across the United States, including PJM.

3 
Antora is a U.S. manufacturer of thermal batteries, which are domestically built in San 
Jose, California, and developer of thermal storage projects for industrial facilities in the U.S. and 
abroad.  
Calibrant develops energy generation and storage assets throughout the United States. 
Calibrant and its partners have developed and expect to continue to develop projects in PJM 
through a range of configurations, including BTMG and co-located projects supporting large 
loads. Specifically, Calibrant has several existing BTMG projects and projects that are currently 
being developed that will be impacted by PJM’s proposed revisions to its Retail BTMG rules.  
Convergent develops, owns, and operates distributed energy storage and storage plus 
solar resources for large commercial, industrial, and utility customers across North American 
markets, including PJM. Convergent has resources in operation and in development in PJM 
including behind-the-meter distribution and transmission connected battery energy storage 
systems, front-of-the-meter distribution connected battery energy storage systems, both with and 
without attached solar systems, and a 20 MW flywheel resource in Hazleton, Pennsylvania.  
Mainspring is a U.S.-headquartered manufacturer of modular, fuel-flexible, and 
dispatchable linear generators, a new type of power generator. Mainspring was founded in 2010 
and its first commercial units were deployed in 2020. The company has been rapidly scaling 
since 2023, deploying its innovative technology across a wide spectrum of customer types and 
use cases. The company’s customers include investor-owned utilities, public power utilities, 
municipal water treatment facilities, biogas facilities, data centers, grocery store chains, cold 
food storage, and hospital systems.  Mainspring’s linear generators can be installed behind a 
customer’s utility meter or as a front of the meter grid asset. Mainspring linear generators are 
currently operating across multiple sites in PJM territory and are in development across

4 
additional sites.Verrus is a developer, owner, and operator of a first-of-its-kind fleet of purpose-
built, load-flexible hyperscale data centers. Verrus designs facilities from the ground up to 
function not only as digital infrastructure but also as grid assets—a new class of large customer 
capable of dynamically adjusting electricity consumption to support reliability, efficiency, and 
affordability. Verrus’ facilities can provide these system benefits without disrupting the critical 
computing workloads that increasingly underpin the modern economy. Each Verrus campus 
integrates on-site utility-scale battery energy storage, advanced load-management controls, and 
grid-aware automation that collectively enable real-time coordination with utilities and regional 
transmission operators.   
Each of the Joint Parties expect to develop storage or generation assets co-located and/or 
behind the meter with loads. They therefore each have a substantial interest in this proceeding 
that cannot be adequately represented by another party. Granting this limited protest will 
critically support development of Co-Located Loads, storage, and BTMG assets that avoid 
“costly and inefficient transmission system buildout.”6 The Joint Parties’ participation is 
therefore in the public interest. 
II. 
LIMITED PROTEST 
A. 
PJM should be required to clarify that an existing interconnection customer 
can nominate a joint withdrawal limit in the Necessary Study process. 
 
Joint Parties seek clarification, consistent with the Request for Clarification that the Joint 
Parties filed in response to the Co-Location Order,7 that PJM’s filing will allow interconnection 
customers serving Co-Located Loads to nominate net withdrawal limitations for purposes of 
these interconnection study processes. This clarification is necessary to realize the Co-Location 
 
6 Co-Location Order, 193 FERC ¶ 61,217 at P 177. 
7 Joint Parties, Request for Clarification, Docket Nos EL25-49-000 & 001, AD24-11-000, EL25-20-000 (filed Jan. 
20, 2026).

5 
Order’s stated intent of ensuring that Co-Located Loads do not pay for services that they do not 
use and do not trigger network upgrades that they do not need.8  
The Co-Location Order is built on the concept that Co-Located Loads can control their 
net withdrawals from the grid, and that market structures should be in place that allow them to do 
so efficiently. The Co-Location Order requires PJM to develop transmission service frameworks 
that allow customers to take as-available service based on the use of special protection schemes 
that enable reliable, as-available service based on technical and engineering requirements set by 
PJM,9 and requires PJM to enable an interconnection customer to request the “minimum level of 
interconnection service it deems necessary.”10   
PJM’s Tariff revisions proposed here, however, appear to remain silent as to how it will 
treat withdrawals in studying Co-Located Load interconnection requests. We therefore seek 
modest clarification from PJM that, to the extent PJM performs interconnection study steps 
involving withdrawal assumptions for Co-Located Loads, an energy storage interconnection 
customer will be able to specify limits to the injection and withdrawal rights reflecting the 
proposed integration of the storage and Co-Located Load facilities. 
Joint Parties submit this protest to preserve their rights and to ensure that PJM does not 
include assumptions in interconnection studies that the load and storage resource withdrawals to 
charge create bluntly overlapping grid impacts (e.g. coincident withdrawals at peak), when in 
fact the storage resources and Co-Located Load could be managed to limit the overall 
withdrawal of the Co-Located Load and to avoid withdrawal when doing so would create grid 
 
8 See, e.g., Co-Location Order, 193 FERC ¶ 61,217 at P 162 (“Collectively, the replacement rate provides pathways 
that recognize Co-Located Loads that limit their energy withdrawals from the transmission system, which may 
require fewer Network Upgrades, and therefore may result in lower Network Upgrade costs as compared to 
requiring all Eligible Customers taking service on behalf of Co-Located Load to take [Network Integration 
Transmission Service].”). 
9 Id. P 212. 
10 Id. P 232.

6 
impacts necessitating network upgrades. Accordingly, Joint Parties request that the Commission 
require PJM to propose narrow Tariff additions to clarify that a Co-Located Load may nominate 
a net withdrawal limit in the same manner that it may nominate a net injection limit.  
a. 
The Commission should require PJM to propose further 
compliance revisions to ensure compliance with the Co-Location 
Order 
 
PJM here proposes Tariff revisions related to Necessary Studies and Necessary Study 
Agreements, including the information needed to perform Necessary Studies.11 PJM does not 
appear to specify in these revisions or elsewhere in the filing how it will treat energy storage 
withdrawals in interconnection studies, or that, to the extent that PJM includes Co-Located Load 
in interconnection studies, interconnection customers may provide withdrawal limits for both the 
energy storage resource components and the Co-Located Load. To remedy these deficiencies, the 
Commission should require PJM to file revisions clarifying that (1) interconnection customers 
may nominate joint withdrawal limits and include information in their requests to modify 
interconnection agreements to demonstrate the ability to operate within such limits; and (2) the 
determination of Network Upgrades, Interconnection Facilities, and any other infrastructure that 
may be required shall account for such limits.  
The Co-Location Order finds the existing PJM tariff unjust and unreasonable because it 
lacks clear provisions to govern the “rates, terms, and conditions of service that apply to 
Interconnection Customers serving Co-Located Load and Eligible Customers taking transmission 
service on behalf of Co-Located Load.”12 The requested revision aims to address precisely this 
defect: the absence of clear rules that govern how Co-Located Load paired with storage will be 
 
11 PJM Filing, Transmittal at 26 (citing Proposed Tariff, Part VII, Subpart A, section 401.H.3.b.i – iii). 
12 Co-Location Order, 193 FERC ¶ 61,217 at P 175.

7 
studied in the generator interconnection process. The Proposed Tariff, as currently drafted, does 
not specify how storage withdrawals will be modeled when a storage facility is seeking to co-
locate with a large load. 
This absence of clear provisions means that without clarification, there is a risk that the 
necessary study process could include assumptions that the load and the charging load of the 
storage resource create bluntly overlapping grid impacts (e.g. coincident withdrawals at peak), 
when in fact the storage resources and Co-Located Load could be managed to limit the overall 
withdrawal of the co-located resource and to avoid withdrawal when doing so would create grid 
impacts necessitating network upgrades. Accordingly, the Commission should require modest 
revisions to clarify that an interconnection customer can nominate a joint withdrawal limit to 
avoid uncertainty. 
b. 
The principles set forth in the Co-Location Order require PJM 
to allow interconnection customers to nominate joint withdrawal 
limits 
 
In the Co-Location Order, the Commission found that “the PJM Tariff is unjust and 
unreasonable because it lacks sufficient clarity and consistency with respect to the rules for Co-
Location Arrangements” and directed changes to the new service request process, as well as the 
necessary study process for modifications to existing facilities.13 With regard to “Interconnection 
Customers seeking to use new generating facilities to serve Co-Located Load,” the Commission 
required PJM to clarify that it “shall consider requests for interconnection service below the full 
generating capability of the generating facility, so that an Interconnection Customer may request 
interconnection service at a level below its maximum facility output to serve Co-Located 
 
13 Id. P 225.

8 
Load.”14 The Co-Location Order aims to minimize infrastructure needs based on interconnection 
customer capabilities including the Co-Located Load’s characteristics, specifying that “[t]his 
revision will clarify that an Interconnection Customer seeking to use a new generating facility to 
serve a Co-Located Load may request only the minimum level of interconnection service it 
deems necessary to effectuate its Co-Location Arrangement.”15  
With regard to the necessary study process, the Commission required PJM “to add to the 
Tariff a description of the scope of the analysis that it will perform as part of the necessary study 
process when an Interconnection Customer seeks to use its existing generating facility to serve 
Co-Located Load,” which must include a description of “the information that the Interconnection 
Customer must provide about the Co-Located Load for purposes of the necessary study.”16 The 
Co-Location Order contemplates that PJM will use this information in determining “any 
modifications or Network Upgrades that are needed as a result of PJM’s study of the change to 
the ISA or GIA to allow the existing generating facility to serve Co-Located Load.”17 And the 
Co-Location Order explains that such upgrades should account for “special protection 
schemes.”18 The implication of these directives is that information about the Co-Located Load 
and special protection schemes may influence what modifications and Network Upgrades may be 
required, because the Interconnection Customer may operate the Generating Facility and Co-
Located Load in a coordinated fashion so as to minimize infrastructure needs. Given the 
ambiguity of the tariff proposed by PJM, we urge the Commission to clarify that such 
information must include the ability to nominate joint withdrawal limits between the Generating 
 
14 Id. P 232. 
15 Id. 
16 Id. P 227.  
17 Id. P 228. 
18 Id.

9 
Facility and Co-Located Load, as such limits may be a critical factor affecting the infrastructure 
that may be triggered by study results where both the Generating Facility and the Co-Located 
Load withdraw electric energy from the system.    
The minor revision we are requesting is necessary to ensure that “the Tariff will have 
sufficient clarity and consistency to facilitate Co-Location Arrangements in a just and reasonable 
and not unduly discriminatory or preferential manner.”19 Just as an Interconnection Customer 
seeking to use a new storage facility to serve a Co-Located Load “may request only the 
minimum level of interconnection service it deems necessary to effectuate its Co-Location 
Arrangement,” similar treatment of an existing Interconnection Customer requires such 
customers to request the minimum level of service necessary to serve the Co-Located Load when 
proceeding through the necessary study process.  
Allowing both new and existing customers the ability to nominate joint withdrawal limits 
is also necessary to give the Co-Location Order’s transmission service reforms meaning. The Co-
Location Order recognizes in the context of requiring PJM to offer non-firm transmission service 
that co-located resources can be integrated so as to “limit [the] energy withdrawals” of Co-
Located Loads in order to prevent “inefficient and costly transmission buildout.”20 In requiring 
PJM to offer Co-Located Loads a menu of transmission service options, the Co-Location Order 
ensures that such loads have the opportunity to receive service that “reflect[s] their actual impact 
on the transmission system.”21 But the value presented by the option to obtain non-firm 
transmission service requires reading PJM’s interconnection service compliance requirements to 
avoid separately forcing Co-Located Loads to bear the cost and delay of unnecessary network 
 
19 Id. P 229. 
20 Co-Location Order, 193 FERC ¶ 61,217 at P 199. 
21 Id. P 162.

10 
upgrades that do not “reflect[s] their actual impact on the transmission system.”22 To achieve the 
objectives of the Co-Location Order, the Commission should therefore require PJM to allow for 
non-firm withdrawal and integrated operation of co-located facilities including net withdrawal 
limits to be integrated into interconnection study assumptions because failing to do so “could 
necessitate inefficient and costly transmission buildout.”23   
B. 
The Commission should reject PJM’s proposed Tariff revisions that preclude 
retail loads served by behind-the-meter generation from taking the new 
transmission services and otherwise limit eligibility for the new transmission 
services to load that is connecting to a generator with interconnection rights.  
 
PJM’s compliance filing is also unjust, unreasonable and unduly discriminatory for 
precluding loads connected to behind-the-meter generation without interconnection rights from 
taking the new Firm and Non-Firm Contract Demand Transmission Services and Interim NITS 
that will be offered to Co-Located Loads. These retail loads are similarly situated to Co-Located 
Loads in their willingness and ability to limit their energy withdrawals from the transmission 
system under certain conditions in the same manner as Co-Located Loads. Just, reasonable, and 
not unduly discriminatory treatment requires that these similarly-situated loads receive similar 
treatment: access to these new transmission service classes.  
The Commission is requiring revisions to PJM’s Tariff with respect to certain BTMG 
loads because such loads “are not fully accounted for in resource adequacy planning and shift 
costs onto other transmission customers.”24 This directive speaks to a desire to render such loads 
visible to the PJM transmission system and require them to pay for transmission service used by 
the load customer that relies on BTMG. The Commission’s stated goals do not suggest a desire 
to force BTMG to move through PJM’s queue even where it does not plan to inject into the 
 
22 Id.  
23 Id. P 199. 
24 Id. P 2.

11 
system, or to require purchase of more transmission service than similarly situated customers. 
Yet, absent removal of the eligibility restrictions proposed by PJM for the new transmission 
services, that is exactly the result that will occur.  
PJM could remedy the deficiency of its proposed replacement rate by removing the 
restrictions on eligibility that allow only Co-Located Loads to access the new transmission 
services. Extending this transmission service eligibility will also further the Co-Location Order’s 
goals of ensuring that loads have the opportunity to receive service that “reflect[s] their actual 
impact on the transmission system”25 and preventing “inefficient and costly transmission 
buildout.”26 
PJM’s compliance filing prohibits retail loads served by “[a]ny facility that qualifies as a 
Retail Behind The Meter Generation . . . from Co-Located Load configurations.”27 By proposing 
to restrict availability of the new transmission services to “Eligible Customers taking 
transmission service on behalf of Co-Located Load,”28 this provision prevents retail customers 
served by behind-the-meter generation lacking interconnection rights from taking the new 
transmission services. These customers are also excluded from new transmission service options 
by PJM’s proposal to define Co-Located Load as “end-use customer load that is physically 
connected to the facilities of an existing or planned Generating Facility on the Project 
Developer’s side of the Point of Change in Ownership to the Transmission Provider’s 
Transmission System.”29 Retail loads served by behind-the-meter generation do not qualify 
under this definition because Generating Facilities under the Tariff must have gone through the 
 
25 Id. P 162. 
26 Id. P 199. 
27 PJM Filing, Transmittal at 7-8 & Proposed Tariff, Definitions – R – S.  
28 PJM, Proposed Tariff, § III. 
29 PJM, Proposed Tariff, Definitions – A - B

12 
interconnection process and have injection rights, which do not apply to behind-the-meter 
generation.30  
PJM’s compliance filing therefore excludes loads served by behind-the-meter generation 
that lack interconnection rights from accessing the new transmission service options despite their 
abilities to limit withdrawals. This result is particularly absurd in light of PJM’s proposal, in 
compliance with the Co-Location Order, to allow Generating Facilities connected to Co-Located 
Loads to nominate net injection limits below their nameplate capacity.31 These provisions would 
enable an interconnection customer to reduce its net injection to 1 MW and receive the new 
transmission services, while prohibiting a BTMG to engage in a nearly-identical arrangement 
that places even less strain on the grid by limiting its net injection to zero (and therefore 
eliminating the need an interconnection agreement for the Generating Facility). 
While PJM’s compliance proposal is generally responsive to the PJM Co-location 
Order’s focus on Co-Located Loads, it does not provide for a just, reasonable, and not unduly 
discriminatory replacement rate with regard to loads connected to behind-the-meter generation. 
Critically, in contrast to the services available to Co-Located Loads, PJM’s proposal does not 
allow customers served by behind-the-meter generation that are similarly situated to Co-Located 
Loads in their willingness and ability to limit withdrawals a similar pathway to use new 
transmission services to limit their impacts on the system.32 Under PJM’s proposal, loads served 
 
30 See PJM, PJM Interconnection, L.L.C./Intra-PJM Tariffs, G-H, OATT Definitions - G - H (9.0.1) (defining 
“Generating Facilities” as “Interconnection Customer’s device for the production and/or storage for later injection of 
electricity identified in the Interconnection Request . . . .”). 
31 PJM, Filing, Docket No. ER26-1088-000, at 4 (filed Jan. 20, 2026) (citing Proposed Tariff, Part VIII, Subpart B, 
section 403 (A)(1)(q) (requiring Applicants, in Generation Interconnection Requests, to “[i]ndicate the level of 
Interconnection Service requested, including whether Project Developer requests Interconnection Service below the 
full generating capability of a new Generating Facility or the requested increase in generation capability of an 
existing Generating Facility to serve Co-Located Load.”)). 
32 The Commission recognized “that Co-Location Arrangements may interact with the transmission system in a 
similar way to BTMG arrangements,” and therefore “sought briefing on how any proposed replacement rate adopted

13 
by behind-the-meter generation must purchase NITS, even where the behind-the-meter 
generation capabilities would allow for use of the more limited transmission services. PJM 
should instead make such services available to other customers with substantively the same 
capabilities to limit withdrawals, including customers served by behind-the-meter generation as 
well as others with inherently flexible demand profiles (such as thermal storage)33 or customers 
located adjacent to generation such that the electrical impacts of the combined load and 
generation are the same with respect to system curtailment needs.34 
The Commission has authority to require PJM to make the new Firm Contract Demand, 
Non-Firm Contract Demand, and Interim NITS services available to loads served by behind-the-
meter generation. In the Co-Location Order, the Commission required PJM to develop BTMG 
rules that address the reliability and resource adequacy risks created by some loads using 
BTMG35 because such loads may “lean on the PJM system when the co-located generation is on 
a full or partial outage or if the load exceeds the rating of the co-located generation.”36 But in 
requiring revised BTMG rules, the Commission recognized “the potential impacts of the 
Commission changing PJM’s BTMG rules for existing BTMG customers,” and therefore 
required PJM to take steps to “minimize the impact of [the BTMG rule] transition on existing 
BTMG customers.”37  
 
in this proceeding would interact with existing BTMG arrangements.” Co-Location Order, 193 FERC ¶ 61,217 at P 
9. Given the delays inherent to interconnecting to the PJM system, obtaining an Interconnection Agreement is likely 
not a viable pathway for most behind-the-meter generators. Moreover, where the load customer behind whose meter 
the generator is connected does not inject into the system, a generator Interconnection Agreement should not be a 
condition of service. 
33 See Antora Energy LLC, Motion to Intervene and Comments, Docket Nos. EL25-49-000, EL25-20-000, & AD24-
11-000, at 3 (filed Apr. 23, 2025). 
34 See Eolian L.P., Initial Comments, Docket No. RM26-4-000, Attach. A at 8 (filed. Nov. 21, 2026) (noting that 
“[C]ases in which the large load is electrically close to the paired generation, metered separately, and not necessarily 
at the same site . . . can provide many of the same benefits as strictly on-site generation and load”). 
35 Co-Location Order, 193 FERC ¶ 61,217 at P 221. 
36 Id. P 186. 
37 Id. P 222.

14 
Importantly, unlike the Commission’s other findings in the Co-Location Order that were 
limited to Co-Located Loads, the Commission’s finding with respect to the BTMG rules “applies 
to all Network Load.”38 The replacement rate must therefore provide for just, reasonable, and not 
unduly discriminatory BTMG rules for all Network Load. This broad finding both requires and 
permits the Commission to require PJM’s replacement rate to allow retail customers who can 
limit withdrawals but who are nevertheless not connected to “Generating Facilities” with 
interconnection rights under the Tariff to take the new transmission services. Alternately, the 
Commission could provide for the same result by granting the PJM Industrial Consumer 
Coalitions pending request for clarification or, in the alternative, rehearing seeking to clarify that 
“[n]ew transmission services outlined in the Order will be made available to retail BTMG 
customers and load-only customers, not just Co-Located Load.”39 Or, the Commission could 
ensure non-discriminatory eligibility for the new transmission services in the Commission’s 
pending paper hearing proceeding in Docket No. EL25-49 et al. to develop the new transmission 
service replacement rate.40  
In the instant proceeding, however, the Commission may not approve PJM’s proposed 
unjust, unreasonable, and unduly discriminatory compliance filing that allows some loads that 
can limit withdrawals to take the new transmission services but denies the same opportunities to 
others with the same technical abilities. Rather, the Commission should reject PJM’s compliance 
filing and direct PJM to allow customers with generation behind their load to access transmission 
services that match their ability to limit withdrawals, similar to customers with load connected to 
Generating Facilities. In the alternative, or in addition, the Commission could defer action on this 
 
38 Id. P 186. 
39 PJM Industrial Customer Coalition et al., Request for Rehearing, Docket Nos. EL25-49-000 & 001, AD24-11,000, 
& EL25-20-000, at 7 (filed Jan. 20, 2026). 
40 Co-Location Order, 193 FERC ¶ 61,217 at P 207.

15 
compliance filing and grant the request for clarification or rehearing arguing that the new 
transmission services must be available to Retail BTMG and load-only customers41 and accept 
this compliance filing after PJM has proposed other revisions to ensure similar transmission 
service access for similarly situated customers.  
III. 
CONCLUSION 
For the foregoing reasons, the Commission should reject PJM’s compliance filing and 
require PJM to: (1) clarify that, in any generator interconnection study process in which PJM 
studies the Co-Located Load’s withdrawals from the grid for purposes of identifying network 
upgrades, including the necessary study process, a Co-Located Load may nominate a net 
withdrawal limit in the same manner that it may nominate a net injection limit; and (2) allow 
loads that can limit their withdrawals similarly to Co-Located Loads to have access to the same 
Firm Contract Demand Transmission Service, Non-Firm Contract Demand Transmission 
Service, and Interim NITS that PJM proposes to provide to Co-Located Loads. 
 
 
Respectfully submitted,

B. The Commission should reject PJM’s proposed Tariff revisions that preclude
